Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )$ (shown above) given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

Evaluating the numerator and denominator at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =1+\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =0-\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the slope of the tangent line to the polar curve $r={e}^{2\theta }$ at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4}$ given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )={e}^{2\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )={e}^{2\theta }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

We have,

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & ={e}^{\pi /2}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\,{e}^{\pi /2},\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & ={e}^{\pi /2}(2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,{e}^{\pi /2},\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /4} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})}{{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\,{e}^{\pi /2})}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,{e}^{\pi /2})} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=2\theta $  at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

We have,

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}+2(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =2+0 \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}-2(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =0-\pi  \\  & =-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /2} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{-\pi } \\  & =-\frac{2}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

For the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ),$ evaluate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4}$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ {x}^{′}(\theta ) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Do not round the answer.

${\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta \,=\,\pi /4}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the rule for differentiating parametric equations:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

Evaluating the numerator and denominator at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-4\cdot 0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-4\cdot 0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-(-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,{|}_{\theta \,=\,\pi /4} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})}{{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =-\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/40375a9794d9e399327cfcf128e017f05d20319fd86d41a8a9f49e01f58ccae0.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=4$  (shown above) at $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =7\pi /4} & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4}) \\  & =-(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

Our strategy will be to compute ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ at $\theta =0,$ and then compute their ratio.

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r={e}^{\theta },$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y={e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ).$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =({e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =({e}^{\theta })^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & ={e}^{\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ), \\  & ={e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $\theta =0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(0) & ={e}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =1\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & =({e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =({e}^{\theta })^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & ={e}^{\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $\theta =0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & ={e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{e}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =1\cdot 0+1\cdot 1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta \,=\,0} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(0)}{{x}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta

$$
x={e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y={e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={({e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & ={({e}^{-3\theta })}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{e}^{-3\theta }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={({e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & ={({e}^{-3\theta })}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-3{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{-3\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={e}^{-3\theta }(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the slope of the tangent line to the polar curve $r = 1-\cos\theta$ at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4},$ given that

$$
y'(\theta) = \cos\theta  - \cos2\theta, \qquad
x'(\theta) = -\sin\theta + \sin2\theta.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the rule for differentiating parametric equations:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

Evaluating the numerator and denominator at $\theta=\dfrac\pi4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /4} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})}{{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Multiplying the numerator and denominator by $2$ and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /4} & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{-\sqrt{2}+2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2-\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2-\sqrt{2}}\cdot \frac{2+\sqrt{2}}{2+\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}+2}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.
$$

Using the fact that $r = 2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /3} & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
